title: Europe’s Ancient Landscapes May Have Been More Open Than We Thought
paragraphs: The popular image of prehistoric Europe as an unbroken, shady wildwood is being questioned by a new synthesis from Aarhus University in Denmark. Rather than leaning on a single record, the team pieced together fossil pollen and plant remains, charcoal from ancient wildfires, chemical signatures in the teeth and bones of herbivores, fossil insects and mammals, and environmental DNA preserved in sediments.

The picture that emerges is of a continent dominated, for well over 20 million years, by a shifting mosaic of trees, clearings and flowering plants rather than by closed canopy. This held under temperate conditions comparable to today’s, as well as in warmer and colder spells. According to the authors, large herbivores such as elephants, rhinoceroses, aurochs and bison were central to the story: by grazing and trampling, they kept the vegetation from closing in.

The implications are not merely academic. Senior author Jens-Christian Svenning argues that current reforestation practices are “on the wrong track”, citing schemes, such as Danish subsidies, that reward only dense forest planting. The team calls instead for restoring woodland-grassland mosaics and bringing back large grazers. As with any synthesis of the fossil record, the evidence is patchy in places, and no single proxy gives a complete picture, which is precisely why several were combined. The findings appear in Biological Conservation.

questions.q: How long did the mosaic landscape last, according to the study?
What role did large herbivores play?
questions.a: They grazed and trampled, stopping the vegetation from closing in.

questions.q: Why were several types of evidence combined?
questions.a: Because no single proxy gives a complete picture.
